text: The Supplier shall indemnify the Buyer against any third-party claim.
Either party may terminate the agreement on thirty days notice.
The Buyer is entitled to a full refund.
The Supplier shall not assign this agreement without consent.
Notice must be given in writing, and a message on the phone is not writing.
Liability is capped at the value of the contract.
The most expensive paragraph in a contract is usually the shortest one.

If you gave me a hundred-page agreement and ten minutes, I would not read the first page. I would go straight to termination, then to the liability cap, then to the governing law, and I would already know more about the deal than somebody who had read forty pages in order. Termination tells me how this ends and what it costs to leave. The cap tells me the size of the worst possible day. The governing law tells me whose rules we are arguing under if it goes wrong. Everything at the front is what the two sides are enthusiastic about, and enthusiasm is the part that changes least in a negotiation. I am not saying skip it. I am saying it is not where the risk lives, and reading it first is how you run out of attention before you get to the paragraph that matters.

The worst mistake I have seen in a translated contract was one word long. The English said that either party may terminate on ninety days notice. The Portuguese version came back saying that either party had to terminate on ninety days notice. Nobody noticed for two years, because for two years nobody wanted to leave. When one side finally did, both companies were reading the same agreement and seeing different obligations, and the argument was not about the business at all. It was about a modal verb. That is why I never translate shall, may and must by feel. Obligation, permission and prohibition are three different commitments, and in English they are three different words. If the person drafting cannot tell you which of the three a clause is doing, the clause is not finished yet.

The agreement arrives and nobody has time to read a hundred pages. The termination clause is read first: how it ends, and what leaving costs. The liability cap and the indemnity are read next, because together they show the worst case. The governing law is checked, because it decides whose rules an argument happens under. And only then are the promises at the front of the contract worth reading.
The Supplier shall indemnify the Buyer against any third-party claim.
Either party may terminate the agreement on thirty days notice.
Notice must be given in writing.
The Supplier shall not assign this agreement without consent.
The Buyer is entitled to a full refund of the price paid.
The Seller is not obliged to accept partial delivery.
Notice must be given in writing, and a message on the phone is not writing.
Liability is capped at the value of the contract.
The most expensive paragraph in a contract is usually the shortest one.
